{{Short description|Special ordered sets}}
In [[mathematics]], '''biquandles''' and '''biracks''' are sets with binary operations that generalize [[racks and quandles|quandles and racks]]. In the theory of [[virtual knot]]s, biquandles are analagous to quandles in the theory of classical [[knot (mathematics)|knot]]s. Biracks and racks have the same relation, while a biquandle is a birack which satisfies some additional conditions.

==Definitions==

A '''birack''' is a set <math> X </math>, two [[Right invertible|right-invertible]] operations <math> \underline{\triangleright}</math><math>, \overline{\triangleright}</math> and a [[bijection]] <math> \pi \colon X \to X </math> such that for all <math> a,b,c \in X</math>,

1.  <math display="inline">\pi(a \overline{\triangleright} a) = a \underline{\triangleright} a</math> and <math> \pi(a) \overline{\triangleright} a = a \underline{\triangleright} \pi(a) </math>. 

2.  The map <math> H \colon X \times X \to X \times X </math> defined by <math> H(a,b) = (b \overline{\triangleright} a, a \underline{\triangleright} b) </math> is invertible.

3. The exchange laws 

* <math> (a \underline{\triangleright} b) \underline{\triangleright} (c \underline{\triangleright} b ) = 
 (a \underline{\triangleright} c) \underline{\triangleright} (b \overline{\triangleright} c ) </math>

* <math> (a \underline{\triangleright} b) \overline{\triangleright} (c \underline{\triangleright} b ) = 
(a \overline{\triangleright} c) \underline{\triangleright} (b \overline{\triangleright} c ) </math>
* <math>(a \overline{\triangleright} b) \overline{\triangleright} (c \overline{\triangleright} b ) = 
(a \overline{\triangleright} c) \overline{\triangleright} (b \underline{\triangleright} c )</math>.

If <math display="inline">\pi = id</math> is the [[Identity function|identity map]], <math display="inline">X</math> is called a '''biquandle.'''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Elhamdadi |first=Mohamed |title=Quandles: an introduction to the algebra of knots |last2=Nelson |first2=Sam |date=2015 |publisher=American mathematical society |isbn=978-1-4704-2213-4 |series=Student mathematical library |location=Providence}}</ref>

Biracks and biquandles were first introduced by Roger Fenn, Mercedes Jordan-Santana and Louis Kauffman in 2004.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fenn |first=Roger |last2=Jordan-Santana |first2=Mercedes |last3=Kauffman |first3=Louis |date=2004-11-28 |title=Biquandles and virtual links |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166864104002044 |journal=Topology and its Applications |volume=145 |issue=1 |pages=157–175 |doi=10.1016/j.topol.2004.06.008 |issn=0166-8641|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
 
Note that the three conditions above correspond directly to the three [[Reidemeister move|Reidemeister moves]] in knot therory, showing the close connections between [[Knot (mathematics)|knots]] and biracks.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Pflume |first=Runa |title=Generalizations of Quandles to Multi-Linkoids |date=2024-04-10 |degree=masterThesis |url=https://ediss.uni-goettingen.de/handle/11858/15204 |doi=10.53846/goediss-10442}}</ref>

== Examples ==
Let <math display="inline">X</math> be a set with two bijection <math>\sigma, \tau \colon X \to X </math> that commute. Then the '''constant action birack''' is defined by <math> a \underline{\triangleright} b = \sigma (a) </math> and <math> a \overline{\triangleright} b = \tau ( x ) </math> and <math> \pi ( a) = \tau^{-1}(\sigma(a)) </math>.

Any [[Racks and quandles|rack]] <math> (X, \triangleright)  </math> is a birack with <math> a \underline{\triangleright} b = a \triangleright b   </math> and <math> a \overline{\triangleright} b = a   </math> for all <math> a, b \in X   </math>. Note that if we insert these operations into the conditions in the definition above, we regain the exact definition of a rack.

Let <math> R  </math> be a [[commutative ring]] with identity and <math> X  </math> an <math> R[s^{\plusmn1}, t^{\plusmn1}] </math>-[[Module (mathematics)|module]]. Then the '''Alexander biquandle''' is defined as <math> a \underline{\triangleright} b = ta + (s-t)b   </math> and <math> a \overline{\triangleright} b = sa  </math>. For <math> s = 1 </math> this is a quandle.
